content: Fordyce's spots, also referred to as Angiokeratoma of the scrotum, Fordyce's disease, Fordyce's spots, or Fordyce granules, are small, painless, raised, pale or white spots or bumps measuring 1 to 3 millimeters in diameter. These spots can appear on the shaft of the penis, the labia, or the inner surface and vermilion border of the lips on the face. They are common in both men and women of all ages. The condition is named after John Addison Fordyce, an American dermatologist. When these spots are located on the head of the penis, they are referred to as Tyson glands, which should not be confused with Hirsuties papillaris genitalis. Fordyce's spots are particularly prevalent in adult males. They may present as a single lesion or as a symmetrical group of up to fifty spots, typically measuring 1 to 2 millimeters in diameter. The exact cause of Fordyce's spots is idiopathic, although there appears to be a genetic predisposition. The condition is not contagious and is not caused by any viruses. While the papules are present at birth, they typically become more noticeable during puberty. Pathologically, Fordyce's spots are a form of ectopic sebaceous glands. They are not associated with any disease or illness and are considered a cosmetic concern only. These spots are non-infectious and represent a natural occurrence on the body. Men often consult dermatologists due to concerns that the spots may be indicative of a sexually transmitted disease (such as genital warts) or cancer, but this is not the case. Additionally, some individuals may be concerned about the appearance of their genitalia and how their sexual partner might perceive it. Diagnosis of Fordyce's spots is typically made through physical examination. No additional diagnostic tests are usually required. Treatment for Fordyce's spots is not medically necessary, as the condition is benign. However, individuals who wish to address the cosmetic appearance of the spots may apply Tretinoin gel or cream to the affected areas daily. This treatment can gradually reverse the condition and prevent it from worsening. For optimal results, Tretinoin can be used in combination with alpha hydroxy acid agents, which are commonly used to treat acne. Vaporizing laser treatments, such as CO2 laser or electro desiccation, have also been employed with some success to reduce the appearance of the spots if they are of cosmetic concern. However, most physicians consider Fordyce's spots a normal physiological phenomenon and generally advise against treatment. In some cases, doctors may prescribe trichloroacetic acid (TCA) chemical peels, but the condition often recurs once treatment is discontinued. Laser vaporization can also be used to remove the spots. Other methods, such as diathermy or liquid nitrogen freezing, may occasionally be employed to address the condition.
